Jessica the jackrabbit wants to climb down a wall. The wall consists of 2026 horizontal layers stacked vertically. The $n$th layer from the top is partitioned into $2^n - 1$ identical rectangular bricks arranged side by side. Jessica begins in the topmost layer, which contains a single brick. A move consists of Jessica going down one layer to a brick that shares a side with the brick she is currently on.

Determine, with proof, the total number of distinct sequences of moves Jessica can take to reach the 2026th layer.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let the common width of the wall be \(1\).  
For layer \(n\), let \(N=2^n-1\), so the \(i\)-th brick from the left occupies the horizontal interval

\[
\left[\frac{i-1}{N},\frac{i}{N}\right].
\]

In layer \(n+1\), there are

\[
2^{n+1}-1=2N+1
\]

bricks. The \(j\)-th brick there occupies

\[
\left[\frac{j-1}{2N+1},\frac{j}{2N+1}\right].
\]

Two bricks in adjacent layers share a side exactly when their horizontal intervals overlap in a nontrivial interval. Thus the \(i\)-th brick in layer \(n\) can move to the \(j\)-th brick in layer \(n+1\) iff

\[
\frac{i-1}{N}<\frac{j}{2N+1}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{j-1}{2N+1}<\frac{i}{N}.
\]

These inequalities are equivalent to

\[
\frac{(2N+1)(i-1)}{N}<j<\frac{(2N+1)i}{N}+1.
\]

Now simplify the bounds:

\[
\frac{(2N+1)(i-1)}{N}=2i-2+\frac{i-1}{N}.
\]

If \(i=1\), this is \(0\). If \(i>1\), it lies strictly between \(2i-2\) and \(2i-1\). In either case, the smallest possible integer \(j\) is

\[
j=2i-1.
\]

Similarly,

\[
\frac{(2N+1)i}{N}+1=2i+1+\frac{i}{N}.
\]

If \(i<N\), this lies strictly between \(2i+1\) and \(2i+2\). If \(i=N\), it equals \(2N+2\). In either case, the largest possible integer \(j\) is

\[
j=2i+1.
\]

Therefore the only possible lower bricks are

\[
j=2i-1,\quad 2i,\quad 2i+1.
\]

All three indeed overlap the current brick, so **every brick has exactly three possible bricks directly below it**.

Jessica must move from layer \(1\) to layer \(2026\), which requires exactly \(2025\) moves. At each move, no matter which brick she is on, there are exactly \(3\) choices.

Thus the total number of distinct sequences of moves is

\[
3^{2025}.
\]

\[
\boxed{3^{2025}}
\]
